p:
I mean, so, it's a great question. Uh, I, and again, it's not that I - I, uh, am unwilling to give the agencies. I just think it would be better to, to have you look at a, a full presentation, uh, that way. I mean, there are, there are disputes, uh, that arise when the public

interacts with members of the government, and that happens across agencies. It could be the Police Department, it could be the Taxi and Limousine Commission. Uh, there are, you know, torts that arise in connection with, uh, potholes. The number of them, as you probably heard in the last couple days, are being filled to avoid that kind of problem. So, you know, I, I think it would be out of context to just say these 3 are the most common problems, because I think what, what I have known from my own time as a civil rights lawyer is that when government and people interact, there's the potential for friction, and then that potential for friction results in potential lawsuits. I see the Law Department's role as not simply defending those cases, but what can we do to minimize that kind of friction between the public and the government.
Your testimony references a number of lawsuits and amicus briefs. Involving federal policy and national issues.
Mmm, mmm.

How does the Law Department decide when it's appropriate for the City

of New York to involve itself in a broader political or policy dispute rather than focusing primarily on defending the city from litigation and protecting taxpayers?

Uh, I, I, I certainly answer that question. I would wanna modify your question slightly, which is to say our determination to get involved with litigation, either if it's us, uh, suing affirmatively or joining in amicus, is when there's a financial interest of the city at stake. So to the extent that funding for Head Start is at risk, or to the extent there's funding, uh, for, ah, housing programs are at risk, those are the kinds of situations that we would wanna make sure that the city's interests are represented, given the potential for substantial loss of dollars for critical city services.
You mentioned—

Just to, you know, give an example, when there was the potential loss of counterterrorism funds, which would have had a tremendous impact, particularly here in Lower Manhattan, uh, that was the kind of case that the Law Department would get

involved in, given the, the financial impact, uh, on a very important city service.

You mentioned litigation related to FEMA reimbursements for services provided to asylum seekers. Uh, can you give us a sense of how much money the city, city's currently seeking to recover and what the Law Department assessment is of our likelihood of actually recovering those funds?

My recollection is that was approximately $80 million, uh, that were dispersed to New York City based upon an act of Congress, uh, and the city has had success at various stages of that case. Uh, you know, in the grand scheme of things, uh, 80— every $80 million counts.

Your testimony also mentions that insurance takeovers have saved the city billions of dollars over time. Are there additional areas where the city could require more robust insurance coverage from contractors or vendors so tax taxpayers aren't left covering litigation costs.
Uh, among the areas that our risk team will be looking at are those, are those kinds of issues.

Obviously, there's a lot of attention, as always, paid to what's going on in the world of social media, and, ah, the Law Department's currently suing several social media companies over youth mental health, um, and other related issues. What specific damages is this, is the city seeking and how confident are you that the city will actually recover meaningful financial compensation?

Uh, any good lawyer would always tell you I'm very confident in the cases that we have pending, uh, and we intend to litigate them vigorously. But they are— again, the city's interest is the cost that the city is paying for services for young people, uh, who, ah, are caught up, uh, in the kind of social media uh, uh, er, efforts that we are addressing in litigation.

Final question. You referenced the continued influx of Adult Survivors Act and Child Victims Act cases. What's the estimated

long-term financial exposure for the city, and how's the Law Department preparing for that?

Yeah, I, I think that, uh, the estimated impact, uh, is uh, something that is still being developed because the cases are still coming in. Uh, and in fact, there were additional, um, additional, uh, modifications that were made in terms of people's ability to file those claims so they still could ripen in the future, as opposed to it was a closed time period and none could be filed. So, uh, projecting the city's potential ultimate, um, uh, financial exposure, uh, it's, it's a literally a moving target given the, uh, ability of people to continue to file those cases. You know, what we're doing about it, as I said in the testimony a little bit earlier, was looking for ways in which we can address the cases that are both, uh, in the city's financial interest, but also respectful of the, uh, real needs of survivors of the kind of conduct that, uh, caused the legislature to initially, originally, um, pass those kinds of acts.
Thank you.
Thanks for those questions.

Thank you. Um, one question I had was the external legal counsel. The plan includes an additional million in intracity funding in 26 only from the Department of Education to extend their use of an external legal counsel contract held by the Law Department by 1 year. The plan also includes another $240,000 of intracity funding in 2 states only from the Department of Environmental Protection to utilize the Department's contract with external legal counsel. Can you talk about these 2, uh, opportunities and situations? What legal matter is, uh, being addressed and why are external law firms required? And do you see a need for further funding in this area?

Well, the one, uh, the environmental protection one is just a good example of, of why, uh, contracts are, are some periodically needed. There's particular expertise in water rights, uh, that are relevant to the kinds of advice and potential litigation support.
Upstate, the Quotin situation. Upstate Quotin?
Uh, no, I think it would be best in a public forum not to get into what exactly the matter is, but it—
Okay, I've been up to Quotin and seen all those.
It's not that one though.
Okay, alright.
Uh, but it involves, uh, particular water right issues that, uh, ultimately the expertise would be really— and will be really important for us in terms of defending the city's interest.
And then there's a DOE also.

Uh, the DOE is— that kind of advice is also relevant to a whole range of different legal matters that they have. Um, there are times when the Law Department will say, we don't have in-house expertise. One of the challenges in the last several years is whether the Law Department had the internal resources, and the additional staffing will help us be able to make judgments uh, about whether to go and get external counsel in fewer instances because we'll have the in-house expertise.
Okay, you talked a little bit—
Sorry, we'll have the in-house resources, so hopefully less outside counsel.
When we have the right resources as opposed to the particularized expertise, uh, which it's more cost-effective to seek outside help than to build expertise that may only be needed periodically.

Okay. You talked about juvenile detention a little bit, but the plan includes an additional $21 million of state funding in 26 that replaces city funding for the Department's role providing support service related to juvenile justice. What role does the Law Department play in juvenile justice, and what is the total amount of funding in the budget for costs associated with juvenile justice? And I think— I didn't know if the state would do this or if it's back to the city. And the reason we ask, of course, there are so many more young people, as you know, in detention than in the past.

Right. I mean, the, the city, the Law Department's role is representing, uh, the city's interest in, in those matters. Uh, the additional state funding is, is part of a state assumption of, um, uh, certain responsibilities in this area. And

those, those dollars will help us continue to provide the services. The family court, as you know, is a court of rehabilitation, uh, and therefore it's particularly important that our lawyers work with the array of services that are available to help, uh, youth move on a path, a positive pathway forward. And that's— the additional resources will help us do that.

So, um, I think we all know a lot of situations that exist in family court. Is that a place where some of your new attorneys might also be situated because it's a very slow process between ACS, et cetera. It's a slow process.

Uh, all across the agency, including the, uh, our, our lawyers that, uh, represent, uh, uh, the agency in family court, that will be one of the areas where we'll be, uh, providing some additional support. As I said at the outset, almost every area of the Law Department suffered, um, pretty significant uh, staffing impact.
Okay.
Over the last 4 years.

We talked about correction a little bit earlier. The plan includes $4.3 million in

city funding in ‘26, increasing to a baseline $9.8 million in '27 for this new manager, which I guess we now have a— from Judge Swayne, we have a name. So how were these amounts determined? Was it just the court? Do you have— gonna need more funding? I guess maybe you don't know. And then, um, you know, how do you, how do you make sure that people are on the remediation manager's team? And I guess also back to the, what you said earlier, fix the problem and then you don't need the remediation. So this is a big challenge.

Well, on this, I would say we've met with the remediation manager. Uh, um, Ms. Neufeld and I have met with the remediation manager, remediation manager, uh, both of us on a number of different occasions. I think that they're, uh, we've met with the remediation manager along with Commissioner, uh, uh, the new DSC Commissioner who we both know, uh, for, for many years. Uh, and I think that this is a good moment to make some progress. Uh, and the remediation manager sees his role as helping us get to a place where, uh, the agency can, uh, operate without a remediation manager. That is a good start.

In terms of setting the level of the funding, it was based upon— in terms of setting the level of funding, it was based upon the remediation manager's desire, uh, to, um, uh, the presentation of what he needed, and ultimately it was with the approval of the court, and the Law Department will be reviewing, uh, the request for payment.

Okay. Um, I know in terms of new needs, just so we're clear, obviously, uh, more attorneys and more support staff. Is that the, the list that you want us to come away with? Of course. Are there any other new needs? If you had your druthers, that you would like to have at the Law Department? Obviously, funding is always the issue.

Ah, ah, having 200 lawyers and 100 support professionals is just a, a really, really important step forward to help, uh, rebuild, uh, the staff from the staffing cuts. And we'll be working with OMB in terms of addressing any needs we have, but also our role in the overall, uh, city efforts to save dollars. So we're gonna be good partners.

Okay and the state budget, obviously there's a Preliminary Governor's Budget, there's a couple of one-house budgets, et cetera. Um,

did you see anything in those that would positively or negatively, um, uh, have any impact on what you're doing? Obviously there's policy in there, there's budget in there, etc. On the state, state level.
I, I think the state budget process is still underway. You and I have both learned from being involved in it over many years that it, it, it's not ended till it's ended.

Okay, okay, because I know we'd love to see some of the money that comes here. Um, and then we heard, we heard a little bit about the federal issues. I am very supportive of what you've been doing, be it Head Start, food stamps, the list is endless. And so I am very supportive of any efforts you can make for us New Yorkers on the federal level, um, in terms of litigation.
Thank you.

Um, but, uh, have you done— I mean, you don't know what's next, what's the next shoe to drop in terms of issues, but do you have any sense of what guidelines— you talked about it a little bit— may impact the city?

And are there any, uh, budget that have been modified in response to changes in federal guidelines? Again, we don't know what's coming next.

Yeah, I, I think, you know, you've answered your own question in a certain regard because we have to be ready. Um, and I've, I've learned in years of as a litigator not to predict what's coming next, but just to be ready for everything.
Okay, okay. Thank you very much, and we look forward to working with you.
Thank you very much. Appreciate everyone's time today.

Next will be the, the Board of Elections. The Board of Elections Fiscal '27 Preliminary Budget totals $146.9 million, which is the same as this budget in the Fiscal '26 Adopted Budget, according to my notes. The Board of Elections is responsible for the implementation of fair and honest elections within the city pursuant to state law, playing a major role in educating New Yorkers on their right to vote and administering elections. The plan includes one new

need of $32.5 million in Fiscal '26 to support election costs in Fiscal '26. I look forward to learning more about the Board of Elections election costs, how early voting locations are selected— always a discussion point— maintaining voter privacy, and how we can increase voting access for justice-involved individuals. And now I'd like to turn it over to be sworn in for the presenters. We will now hear testimony from, uh, the Board of Elections. Before we begin, I will administer the affirmation. Panelists, please raise your right hand. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this Committee, and to respond honestly to Council Member questions?
I do, yes.
Okay, you may begin when ready.

Thank you. Uh, good afternoon, uh, Chair Brewer and, uh, Councilman Morano. Um, my name is Michael Ryan. I'm the executive director of the Board of Elections, uh, and joining me today, uh, is the board's, uh, deputy executive director Vincent, uh, Ignizio, who is well known to this body as well.

Um, we have prepared testimony. We've submitted the written testimony. Uh, we're prepared to rely on the written submission if that, uh, is the— sits well with the, uh, uh, with Madam Chair and move on to, uh, any questions that the, uh, Committee members may have.
Go ahead and read your testimony. That's fine. So the public knows what you're saying. Yep.

Okay. So, um, we'll review the 2026, uh, Fiscal Year, which we, which we, uh, always do in our budget testimony. Um, we want to thank the Mayor's office, uh, and the City Council for providing the necessary, uh, support to the board for Fiscal Year 2026. Uh, that funding met the constitutional and statutory mandates as well as the needs of the voters of the City of New York. I extend, uh, a special, uh, thank you for addressing the board's funding needs, uh, during these very difficult times. Uh, in FY 2026, the board conducted several election events, including the mayoral general election conducted on November 4th, uh, 2025, special elections for the State Senate District 47, New York

State Assembly Districts 36 and 74, uh, conducted on February 3rd, 2026. Uh, we will conduct another special election for the 3rd Council District on April 28th, 2026, and the June primary for federal and state offices. Uh, each of these election events includes 9 days of early voting. Um, uh, the board successfully maintained 156 voting sites across all 5 boroughs, um, under the Make Voting Easy Act, ensuring accessible voting for all contests. In Fiscal Year 2026, the board managed multiple election events with significant turnout, uh, across the general election and primary— primary and special elections, and total operating expenses uh, estimated at $263 million, which would include personal services of $126 million and other than personal services of $137 million. Poll workers and related seasonal costs represented a major factor, followed by leases, services, printing, and transportation. Voter outreach generated substantial impressions throughout various media channels and operations maintained at the 156 early voting sites with minimal equipment issues. The board complies with the New York State election law requirements for mail ballot canvassing

requiring extended public access, uh, prior to Election Day. The statewide online mail ballot application and tracking portal, online voter registration, and automatic voter registration initiatives such compliance has ongoing effects on, uh, or ongoing budget and fiscal implications. The board works closely with the Office of Management and Budget, uh, to manage these mandates and finalize funding for all elections. Uh, in addition, the board works very closely, uh, with the New York State Attorney General to ensure full compliance with the New York State uh, Voter Rights Act, which is also known as the John Lewis Voter Rights Act. Moving on to Fiscal Year 2027, uh, again, the board expresses its gratitude to the city Administration and the City Council, uh, for partnering with the board. For Fiscal Year 2027, the board projects, uh, potentially a budget of $280 million to meet the demands of major statewide election cycle addressing critical infrastructure upgrades. Uh, the board is requesting $130 million to be allocated to personal services and $150 million to be

added— allocated to OTPS, including, uh, one-time capital investments. In FY 2027, the board will conduct two major election events, November 3rd, 2026, general election, uh, for, uh, governor and lieutenant governor and other statewide, uh, congressional, uh, and congressional offices, and a primary election on June 22nd, 2027. Each event includes 9 days of early voting. Conducting early voting for a continuous 9-day period has fundamentally altered the board's approach to elections transitioning from single-day events to 10-day operations over approximately 2 weeks, maintaining the 156 early voting sites necessitates additional funding for equipment, office space, staff training, leasing, poll site costs, and public education to meet increasing demands from statewide contests and citywide contests. The budget also includes essential upgrades and enhancements to ensure reliable, secure, and accessible elections. Um, replacement of 2,287 ballot marking devices and potentially upwards of 700 more, uh, at an estimated $8,000 per unit, and additional ancillary equipment totaling approximately $30 million. Uh, this addresses end-of-life concerns,

memory limitations, and compatibility issues in the current fleet, ensuring full accessibility for voters with disabilities, ah, and compliance with the Help America Vote Act requirements and supporting high turnout in statewide elections. It must be clearly noted that replacement of the BMDs BMD devices compatible with the board's current voting machines have not been certified by the New York State Board of Elections. Uh, and the board is not permitted to use any BMDs unless the New York State Board of Elections completes its certification process. Accordingly, the board is providing this information to advise that we have been informed that the certification process is underway and anticipated to be completed at the end of Fiscal Year 2026. Upon certification, the board intends to submit replacement costs as a new need during Fiscal Year 2027. Um, further, with respect to technology issues, to ensure compatibility with Windows 11, uh, and continued enhancement of cybersecurity security, uh, all computers utilized by the board, and I believe other city agencies as well, must be replaced.

The cost for such replacement is estimated at up to $8 million. This includes workstations, administrative systems, and to prevent vulnerabilities, support mo— modern voter registration slash absentee portals, and maintain secure operations. Um, we'll also have to replace some vehicles. Replacement of 4 aging Sprinter vans used for transporting, uh, voter equipment and supplies that are utilized by the borough offices. Uh, although we have 5 borough offices, only 4 are presently eligible for replacement, and that estimated cost is between $300,000 to $500,000. These vehicles are critical for logistics across, uh, the 1,200— more than 1,200 Election Day locations and the 156 early voting sites, as well as regular business conducted between the boroughs, uh, particularly during extended early voting periods and multiple, uh, event cycles. The board is working with DCAS to finalize the approval process for the purchase of the vehicles, uh, that fully meet the needs— the board's operational needs. These capital investments coordinated with the Office of Technology, uh, and Innovation and fleet management protocols are vital

to prevent disruptions, uh, in the 2026 gubernatorial cycle and align with ongoing mandates for secure, accessible voting. The board is committing to phasing, uh, these in where possible, uh, to manage fiscal impact. Uh, the board will continue appropriate outreach to voters and poll workers. The board reaffirms its request to establish municipal poll workers— uh, a municipal poll workers slash a municipal workers slash poll workers program. Uh, ongoing voter education remains essential. The board will implement media campaigns in partnership with groups like the Campaign Finance Board for message, message consistency and board coverage, uh, building on successful outreach, uh, in prior elections, uh, cycles. Excuse me, I just need a little water. Uh, expanded early voting heightens cybersecurity needs. The board maintains ongoing monitoring and a strong relationship, uh, with OTI. The New York State, uh, Board of Elections directs enhanced requirements necessitating additional staffing. The board must implement an internal cybersecurity staff task force with added staff, including, uh, potential TIGR grant, uh, support. And OTI, when it was, uh, in its

prior iteration as NYC3, Uh, provided the contractual, uh, mechanism that allows the board to have external 365 by 24 by, by, by 7 by 24 monitoring of all of us, uh, all of our, uh, systems and, uh, and servers, uh, so that we, we, we work, uh, at preventing any cybersecurity, uh, breaches. Uh, the board is committed to working closely with its government partners and interested parties to effectively serve the voters of the city of New York. Uh, any resources will be used responsibly to meet the needs of the voting public. The board remains sensitive to the fiscal challenges of New York City and mindful of its obligations. The board is committed to the partnership with the Administration and the Council. The board is confident that additional funding requests, including essential upgrades, will enhance our ability to serve the voters. The board reaffirms its commitment, uh, that allocated resources will be used wisely, uh, and the public trust will continue to be a guidepost. Uh, and now myself and Mr. Ignizio, uh, will be happy to answer any questions that the Committee may have.

Oh, thank you. I'll ask some. I'm sure my colleague from Staten Island will have some for you also. Um, the— what— I know you talked about the need for these new machines whenever it gets certified by the state, etc. Um, so what capital request is the department, uh, the board making to OMB now? Is it— are we doing the— starting with the machines? We don't even know what machines we're getting.

Right? What we have done to this point is basically indicated to OMB that we're anticipating a new need ask. We can't make the ask, as, uh, the Chair rightly points out, until the machines are certified. We have been given other dates in the past when the certification process would have been completed. Um, those dates were not met. B-but where we, we have received assurances that it is on, uh, a better path now and that they're expecting to certify, uh, by the end of the year. Keep in mind that that's not just within, um, within the ambit of the State Board of Elections. It requires, um, cooperation from the vendor, and the vendor must meet, uh, its mile markers as well, because all of these technological, uh, equipment

that is related to elections all gets, uh, verified through an outside lab to check that all of the coding, uh, is done properly and works effectively.

And, and Mike, if I could, if I could add, Madam Chair and to the Committee, the— there is an international RAM shortage, uh, across, across the globe right now due to the AI technology, and it's sucking up all the excess, uh, RAM that's going on across in the world. So the company itself would need to ramp up in order to meet the needs of a large order that we would place here for New York City. So what we're trying to do is encourage our friends at the, at the State Board of Elections to work with us such that we have the runway sufficient to have them ready, um, have them in place by a 2028, uh, year. So that's the goal. Because we're New York City, because we're so large, we have— we need a lot longer runway than a smaller county upstate would and we're hopeful to be able to provide these BMDs to our accessible community.
And do the upstate folks have the same BMDs? They have the same—
Yeah-
They would be a statewide contract, I assume. Is that how it works?
Yeah, they, they would be approved and then they can buy— the counties can buy them at, at, at—
And to the extent that they have the same vendor that we have.
That's what I'm asking.
Right, if they have the same vendor that we have, then they have the same problem.
Right.
But they're buying 10. We're— but, you know, all due respect to our friends at Oneida and Onondaga County, they're buying far fewer than we are.

Okay and is there any discussion about what kind of machines? There's always a discussion down here. I mean, is it just up to the state? Do they take import from the people who are going to be using them down here?
They do the certification.
And you know here's always a lot of drama about the machines that are purchased.

They do the certifications, and we require machines that would actually speak to our machines as well. So, um, not ones that just— so we would— we are required to purchase what those that have been certified by the State Board of Elections.
Okay.
And, and Madam Chair-
Having been through this before?
Right. This is going to be about, uh, you know, a roughly a $30 million expenditure.
Okay.
And that's only for the BMDs.
Right, I understand.
And that would be leaving our current voting machines in place.
Right?
So to give that, you know, uh, a perspective of scale, if we were to at some point down the road replace the voting machines themselves, we would be talking about a far greater—
Oh, I know.
Uh, expenditures.
But I'm just saying, even within the disabled community, which is something that we're talking about, they always have what they like and what they don't like. So that's why I was asking.

So, so I, I think the reason for us, uh, bringing this up today and making sure that we stress it now is so that we don't sneak up on the fiscal planners for the City of New York, number one, which would be unfair. But number two, to let the, the, uh, accessibility community know that we are thinking of them. We acknowledge that the current ballot marking devices are not meeting their needs, and we're doing everything we can to be prepared, uh, to meet their needs better when the new machines are, are able to be utilized.
Okay, I'm— I just— we've all been through this before, so I didn't want to go through it again. Are there other requests that will be— obviously this is not immediate— going to OMB for capital?

Um, the vehicles that we referred to that are, that are at their, their life,

uh, lifespan, we will be requesting of those but that's it for, for, um, additional needs.

Right, you talked about those? Okay. I was thinking about some of the— I mean, I don't know, they're not as expensive, but you always need— I don't know what you call them— gangplanks to get from one end of the non-accessible, uh, area to another. You know, sometimes you need those long—
Are you referring to our ramp contracts?
I call them gangplank.
Yeah, yeah, we, we, I think we have approximately 17 vendors that provide for RAMP contracts.
And those are capital or that's—
That's expense.

That’s expense money. I mean, we, we've encouraged several times to work with both the— all of our providers to see if we could have capital improvements that meet the requirements that we wouldn't need them. And that can— those

conversations are ongoing for every school whenever they come up, or for whatever library.
And obviously our preference would be for all of the buildings, uh, that we utilize to be, uh, permanently accessible.
Accessible for your guidelines.
Right, right.
Towards our standards, yeah.
But we do what we have to do.
No, I know.
And that's all coming out of expense money.

So along those lines, obviously there's, uh, the lab school on the east side is the one that sends me many emails, and there are probably other schools. I know you'd love to get out of the school business, I understand that it's hard to find other places. So my question is twofold. One, in that particular instance, um, they had suggested some nearby cultural institutions. I know you were kind enough to make that change on the Upper West Side where we went to the American Museum. Um, so I'm just wondering, in that particular situation,

is there movement to find another place? This is the Lab School.
Yeah so-
And then also just generally, how can we help you get out of some of these schools?

So, uh, the umbrella is out of 158, uh, schools that will be— 158 early voting sites, about 25% of them are schools. We would love to be out of them as much as possible. We reach out to Council Members, we reach out to market makers and say, please provide us with, uh, ideas on how we can, can do so. The problem once again is the runway. We can't decide in 2026 that in for this primary or for the general we're going to switch and move and into a different location. So that's always been an issue, and finding suitable sites that are accessible, that do have the ability to hold a polling site and the requirements they're in, is not as easy. With regards to this specific site, the— I might say it wrong— the, the, is it the Rubin Museum?
Yes.
Our understanding is that that building was sold and unavailable, uh, it has been surveyed and there was a second suggestion which -
I— I think it was the Whitney.

Which I don't know much about the Whitney, um, and/or we have— but we have, you know, I, I work very closely with the Deputy Chancellor Kevin Moran, as does Mike, and we have a great relationship to try to accommodate. But we would like to be clear, we would like to be out of schools as well. We just need a suitable alternative to do so. So we'll review the Whitney Museum, um, and have our—
They’re suggestions I mean, after 400 or 500 emails, I'd love to work with you to try to find something else because—
Happy to—
They come in every day.
Happy to.

And Madam Chair, uh, quite frankly, uh, you have worked with us, uh, in your former capacity as the Borough President as well, and, and

we, and we appreciate that because we really do believe that the elected officials in practical reality are and should be the eyes and ears of the community. Uh, and to the extent that there's, uh, information that we're missing or a potential, uh, blind spot, we're happy for that to be pointed out to us and, and work to make, uh, any necessary corrections.
I know my friend Dan Slippin is gonna want a shout out right now, so thank you to the Met for being a, a, a very good neighbor with regards to moving the cipher.
Definitely deserves it. I yield to my, uh, counterpart from Staten Island.

Thank you, Madam Chair. It's always a treat to see, uh, two Staten Islanders at that table, and a special treat when one of them is not only a former member of this body but a former representative of the 51st Council District.
And the best man at your wedding.

Naturally. Oh, hey, I I didn't wanna— I didn't wanna out you. Um, according

to the Mayor's, um, Preliminary Budget Report, uh, complaints about— and Management Report, uh, complaints about poll workers dropped from 551 in Fiscal Year 2023 to just 90 in Fiscal Year 2025, which is obviously a pretty dramatic improvement. What changes did the board actually implement in either training, management, or whatever else that led to that reduction?
Let me point out that I was hired in 2022.

Well, uh, apparently, uh, it was all related to, uh, Mr. Ignizio's arrival, uh, but truthfully, we, um, our recruiting, uh, program that we've implemented, uh, which of course we usually utilizing social media and all the other, you know, tools that are available uh, has been, uh, a very, uh, has been more robust than it had been in the past. And, and to keep, uh, to keep the, uh, public kind of misperception, uh, that the Board of Elections is this, you know, only political things happen at the Board of Elections, the number of percentage of poll workers that come directly from political parties has been dropping steadily from, uh -
That’s a good I’m sorry.

During my 13 years through no specific effort other than the fact that it's just dropping steadily. And I think we're under 25% of the poll workers come directly from the political parties and 75% come from interested citizens who go on to electiondayworker.com and wanna sign up to help the community. So I think that, you know, taking it away from us, taking responsibility for all the great things and flipping it back to the community, I think we do have a lot more community interest, uh, in people wanting to serve and taking pride in that service. So yes, our training has improved, all of those things that you would expect that would lead to it, but we also have a lot of a lot of public interest, and that's, uh, I think the poll workers need to be praised for that.

Frank if I, if I can add, we, we have, we have a very professional staff. The stat— the, um, New York City Board of Elections has the only CIRA-certified office of managers in the entire country. Um, so while it's fashionable sometimes to throw shots at it, uh, we're very proud of the

management team we've assembled. They are CIRA-certified certified, the only in the state. They are doing a fantastic job, and good management ends up being, uh, you'll see it in the, in the product. And I think many people, including those in the, uh, those that have bashed, continually bashed the Board of Elections, have seen a noticeable difference of quality elections that were served to the people of the City of New York over the last several years. So we're proud of it. We're gonna, uh, continue to build on it but we have so many people who want to serve uh, we have more poll worker requests than we do, uh, slots for them because people want to be a part of, of the civic process, and we, we welcome it.

Since you both mentioned the changes in poll worker recruitment and everything else, again, according to the Mayor's, uh, Preliminary Management Report, it shows that poll worker attendance on Election Day has remained above 96%, which is obviously pretty impressive. Given the size of the system. The— what strategies has the board used to recruit and retain such a reliable poll worker workplace, given, as you said, the decrease in direct referrals from the political parties?

Well, the, the public's been very generous with their money as well. They're, they're paying poll workers now $2.50 for the day and $3.50 for coordinators, so that does attract people as well. People wanna be more engaged, and I think every time that there is a major race, you know, a mayoral race, a presidential race. People are more interested in getting involved, and, and that's been great. And, you know, we've had a— we've had a very good team of, of, uh, folks that have been getting the word out about what's going on at elections, and people just want to get involved.

You know, speaking about the swings in turnout, I'll ask you both this, Mr. Ryan. The, the Mayor's Management Report shows huge differences in turnout depending on the election cycle. Whether we're talking a Mayor's race, a presidential race, or a City Council race. How does the board scale staffing and logistics to handle those large swings in voter participation?

What we have— what we have done is we treat every election event— but when I was talking citywide election events, we treat every citywide

election event as if there's going to be 100% turnout. So we don't have large fluctuations in terms of, say, the number of poll workers. Because, you know, the analogy that I use is if you're going to throw a party and you're going to invite 100 guests, you have to buy all the food for 100 guests, you have to buy all of the paper goods for 100 guests. And if only 10 people show up, you might have a lot of leftovers, uh, but you still were prepared for the 100 people that you invited. And, and that's what election events are. We have to prepare as if 100% of the voters are going to turn out. Now, that having been said, we recognize that in this order—presidential followed by gubernatorial followed by mayor and then followed by the Queens DA and the Staten Island DA—you know, those are our, uh, highest to lowest, uh, election, uh, events. And that hasn't changed, although the numbers within you know, some presidential years are more robust than others, but in terms of that order, that pecking order, that hasn't changed in the, in the 13 years that I've been here.

Uh, the Chair asked you about early voting, and you mentioned in your testimony that early voting has effectively transformed elections from this single-day event into roughly a, a 10-day operational period. How has the board adapted its planning and staffing to manage an expanded time frame like that?
